The key thing to realize is that you operate on a commonsense notion of truth, i.e. correspondence of truth with facticity - what you see is true and what is true is a fact of reality. That isn't how perception works. It's fuzzier.

The angle of light entering the eye determines where it is coming from geometrically in your field of perception, hence determines the location of its source. You are essentially seeing the sun through a filter that is altering the angle of that light the closer that the sun approaches the horizon. The closer the sun is overhead, the more accurately you are seeing it's true position. But near the horizon the angle of the light causes you to perceive the sun in an apparent position that is the most deviant from it's real one.

Now think about that in terms of objects you see at large distances - i.e. where earth's curvature would also place them close to your perceptual horizon line. It's the same idea. Of course, this all depends upon the source of sunlight (location of the sun) relative to the system of viewer and viewed object. But the concept is similar. Light reflected off of that object is being refracted through layers of different density of atmosphere. It isn't so much about it's absolute path as it is about the angle and frequency at which it enters your eye.

This also has to do with the reason the effect is more pronounced over large bodies of water. It is also responsible for mirage effects.
